<reason>Both sides opened strongly, but B built a more concrete and resilient case. B anchored its position in specific, plausible touchstones (the 2008 Ilulissat Declaration, the 2010 Norway-Russia Barents Sea boundary resolution, the binding Polar Code, CLCS adjudication) that directly served as counter-evidence to A's core claim that competing claims inevitably produce an arms race and ungoverned gaps. A's rebuttal to the Ilulissat "no" relied on an underdeveloped "deadlock itself will force yes" mechanism that B's closing correctly identified as unproven — a decade of actual deadlock has produced the opposite. Similarly, A's answer to the demilitarization/nuclear-deterrent pressure point mostly re-asserted the 1959 Antarctic analogy without engaging B's sharper distinction (Antarctica had no strategic assets or population; the Arctic's under-ice patrols are Russia's second-strike deterrent). Critically, B's Rebuttal 2 introduced the concrete Barents Sea counter-example after A's own Rebuttal 2, and A's closing never directly engaged it, leaving a live rebuttal unanswered at the final juncture. A's framing ("what rules reward," precaution over carve-up) was rhetorically vivid and the debate's most original throughline, but it didn't overcome B's grounded feasibility and necessity attacks. B therefore ends with the cleaner, more decisively unrebutted path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 citing the 2010 Norway-Russia Barents Sea resolution as proof that overlapping claims can be resolved under existing law without a comprehensive treaty — a concrete counter to A's core "competing claims force conflict" narrative that A's closing never directly answered.</best_rebuttal>
